abstract: Throughout biology, RNA molecules form complex networks of molecular interactions that are central to their function, and which play important roles in organizing cellular architecture. But, there are few robust tools available for probing these interaction-networks in situ. Here, we introduce Oligonucleotide-mediated proximity-interactome MAPping (O-MAP), a straightforward method for elucidating the biomolecules near an RNA of interest, within its native context. O-MAP uses RNA-FISH-like oligonucleotide probes to deliver proximity-biotinylating enzymes to a target RNA in situ , enabling nearby molecules to be enriched by streptavidin pulldown. This induces exceptionally precise, RNA-targeted biotinylation that can be easily optimized and ported to new targets or sample-types. Using the noncoding RNAs 47S, 7SK, and Xist as models, we develop O-MAP workflows for discovering RNA-proximal proteins, transcripts, and genomic loci. This enabled first-of-its-kind, multiomic characterization of these RNAs’ subcellular compartments, revealing new regulatory interactions. O-MAP requires no genetic manipulation, uses exclusively off-the-shelf parts, and requires orders of magnitude fewer cells than established methods, making it accessible to most laboratories.
